commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether obtaining vendor validation evidence and independently verifying claims leads to better local performance or fewer harms, so the recommendation rests on expert consensus from 14 sources and on three studies showing that vendor claims often exceed measured performance. In those studies, vendor-reported accuracy averaged 91.5% against 67.3% in real-world use, and a second vendor model and a proprietary risk score also fell short of their reported figures.

perspectives.view: No included study compares sites that verified vendor claims with sites that did not. The three hazard studies use descriptive, pre-post, or simulated designs at levels 3 and 4. They consistently show a gap between claimed and measured performance, but they cannot show that local verification closes that gap or changes outcomes.

A mean gap of 24.2 percentage points (95% CI 21.5 to 26.9) across six systems suggests that a tool chosen on vendor figures alone may miss or misclassify many more patients than expected. Pre-deployment verification is a plausible way to catch this before patients are exposed, though no study confirms that it does.

In a study of 599,163 emergency department visits, a vendor model's performance differed substantially from vendor-reported metrics once it was tailored for real-world use. This suggests that verification may need to take place in the configured local workflow, and that checks against the vendor's reference data alone may be insufficient.

A study of six systems in rural Nigeria covering 52,000 patients found gaps of 17 to 35 percentage points, significant for every system. An opioid risk score also underperformed on California PDMP and commercial claims data even with socioeconomic covariates added. These findings suggest that vendor validation cohorts may not reflect the populations a health system serves.

The radiology multi-society statement notes that vendors test tools during regulatory approval but still advises local validation before clinical use. The endorsing sources treat regulatory clearance as insufficient on its own. The supplied studies do not examine whether cleared and uncleared tools differ in the size of the performance gap.

One endorsing report describes health systems that support pilots but lack the analytics and measurement tools to assess impact. Independent verification therefore requires data, staff time, and methods that many systems may not have. No supplied study reports the cost or staffing needed to verify a vendor tool.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares deployment outcomes, local performance, or patient harms between health systems that independently verified vendor claims before purchase and those that relied on vendor documentation. Studies are also needed on which verification methods, sample sizes, and comparability criteria predict local performance, and on what verification costs.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population. One hazard study was conducted in rural Nigeria and found gaps of 17 to 35 percentage points, but none of the studies reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. How far vendor claims diverge from measured performance for these groups in U.S. settings therefore remains unknown.
